title: Generative AI in Learning Design Practice: Building an Online Course for Biomedical Sciences Research Programs
venue: International Journal of Designs for Learning
extended_summary:
This design case examines how a multidisciplinary instructional design team integrated generative AI tools into the creation of a self-paced online course on program evaluation for biomedical sciences research training programs. The paper asks how GenAI can support different stages of instructional design — from needs analysis and objective refinement to script drafting, image creation, assessment development, and multimedia production — while still preserving human judgment, pedagogical quality, accessibility, and ethical responsibility.

The intervention was not a learner-facing AI tutoring system; rather, it was an AI-supported design workflow. The team used tools such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Canva, Audiate, Camtasia, and H5P within Moodle to develop seven online modules covering evaluation concepts, design, data collection, ethics, and reporting. They also used AI to simulate a learner needs interview, generate draft objectives and scenarios, and draft quiz items and narration, then revised all outputs through SME review, user testing, and external evaluation.

The intended audience included program directors, training grant managers, administrative staff, faculty, and graduate students in biomedical sciences at Iowa State University and similar contexts. The course was designed for asynchronous online delivery because target learners had busy and variable schedules. The case concludes that GenAI can improve efficiency and help structure design thinking, but its outputs were often inaccurate, repetitive, contextually weak, or ethically problematic, requiring substantial human oversight. The authors argue that GenAI should be treated as a scaffold rather than a replacement for instructional expertise.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI tools used for drafting, revising, and producing instructional content, assessments, visuals, and audio narration.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as co-thinkers in the instructional design process for a self-paced online course, including brainstorming, learner persona simulation, objective refinement, script drafting, image/layout generation, audio narration, assessment drafting, and accessibility support.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI tools accelerated ideation, drafting, and multimedia production, helping the team produce module content, scripts, visuals, and audio narration more quickly. However, the authors repeatedly note that substantial human revision was still required, and in some cases revising AI output took as long as writing from scratch.
findings.measure: Design workflow efficiency and production support (qualitative design reflections)

findings.finding_summary: GenAI supported early-stage learner analysis, objective drafting, and accessibility brainstorming, but the paper emphasizes risks including inaccuracies, distorted or misspelled outputs, limited contextual understanding, copyright/privacy concerns, and unclear transparency around AI-generated content. The team concluded that human oversight, SME review, and ethical guardrails were necessary throughout.
findings.measure: Reported risks and ethical/design issues during course development (qualitative reflection)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a design case and reflective report rather than an empirical evaluation of AI effectiveness, so it does not meet criteria for higher evidence tiers. The paper provides practice-based observations but no controlled comparison, quantitative effect estimates, or outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical workflow benefits from GenAI for instructional design efficiency, but the gains are qualitative and not quantified. It also documents meaningful risks and limitations, so the overall impact is positive but modest and mixed.
